intents.summary_en: Phishing is a deceptive social engineering attack where cybercriminals impersonate reputable organizations or colleagues to steal credentials, money, or sensitive data.
action_steps_en: Inspect the sender's actual email address (not just the display name) for typosquatting (e.g., @micros0ft.com or @paypal-security-alert.net).
Look for artificial urgency ('Account suspended in 24 hours!', 'Immediate wire transfer required').
Hover over hyperlinks (without clicking) to inspect the actual destination URL.
Never open unsolicited attachments, especially archives (.zip, .rar, .iso) or macro-enabled documents.
Verify suspicious requests via a secondary, trusted communication channel (call the person or visit the official website directly).
red_flags: Generic greetings ('Dear Customer') when they should know your name.
Urgent threats of account closure, legal action, or fines.
Requests for passwords, gift cards, wire transfers, or MFA codes.
Mismatched URLs that don't match the company's real domain name.
responses_en: Phishing relies on impersonation, artificial urgency, and deceptive links. Always check the true sender domain, hover over links before clicking, and verify unexpected requests through an independent channel.
Urgent messages and unexpected links are common phishing tactics. Verify through a trusted channel.
Use the official delivery service to check a parcel; don't trust unsolicited payment links.
Unexpected prizes that require upfront payment are a common scam warning sign.
Lookalike sender addresses can impersonate trusted organizations. Verify the exact address and request.
Unexpected attachments can contain malware. Confirm with the sender using a known contact method.
Fear and urgency are used to make people click fake login links. Navigate to the service independently.
Changing the exposed password promptly limits misuse; also enable MFA and report the incident.
Compromised or spoofed accounts can impersonate colleagues. Verify unusual requests separately.
Recovery codes are sensitive credentials. Only use them on the genuine service you navigated to yourself.
Reporting helps security teams block similar messages and protect other people.

intents.pro_tip_en: When in doubt, never click the email link. Open your browser, type the official website URL manually, and log in from there.

patterns_en: Difference between phishing and spear phishing
intents.summary_en: Spear phishing is a highly targeted attack where adversaries research a specific individual or company (using LinkedIn, social media, or company websites) to craft convincing, personalized lures. Whaling specifically targets senior executives, directors, or finance personnel.
action_steps_en: Be aware that attackers can cite your real job title, coworkers' names, and current projects.
Establish dual-control out-of-band authorization for any financial transaction or vendor bank detail changes.
Scrutinize requests coming from lookalike executive domains (e.g., ceo-office@company-corp.com instead of company.com).
Limit the amount of sensitive business and organizational hierarchy data shared publicly on social media.
red_flags: Emails claiming the CEO is in an 'urgent meeting' and cannot take phone calls.
Requests to bypass standard purchase order or invoice verification protocols.
Direct requests for employee W-2 forms, payroll accounts, or employee databases.
responses_en: Spear phishing uses tailored personal information to lower your guard. Whaling targets executives and finance teams to execute fraudulent wire transfers. Always verify out-of-band using an established phone number.
intents.pro_tip_en: If a high-level executive asks you to break normal security protocol, that urgency itself is the #1 indicator of spear phishing.

patterns_en: Received weird SMS asking to verify account
intents.summary_en: Smishing is phishing conducted via SMS text messages, while Vishing is voice phishing conducted over phone calls or automated voice bots. Both aim to induce immediate panic.
action_steps_en: Never click links inside unexpected text messages—even if the sender claims to be USPS, UPS, your bank, or Netflix.
Legitimate banks will NEVER call or text you demanding your one-time SMS verification passcode or debit card PIN.
If someone calls claiming to be from IT support, law enforcement, or your bank, hang up immediately.
Call the institution back using the official phone number printed on the back of your card or on their official website.
red_flags: Texts regarding 'Unclaimed package', 'Suspended debit card', or 'Overdue toll fees' containing shortened URLs.
Callers with urgent or aggressive tones demanding immediate payment via gift cards or wire transfers.
Callers asking you to read back a verification code sent to your phone.
responses_en: Smishing (SMS) and Vishing (phone calls) exploit mobile convenience and urgency. Never click links in unprompted text messages and never read one-time passcodes over the phone.
intents.pro_tip_en: Forward suspicious SMS messages to spam reporting code 7726 (SPAM) on major mobile carriers to help block the campaign.

intents.summary_en: Business Email Compromise (BEC) occurs when an attacker compromises a real corporate email account or spoofs a trusted vendor/executive to trick employees into transferring funds or revealing proprietary information.
action_steps_en: Institute a strict policy: Any change in vendor banking details requires verbal voice confirmation with known contacts.
Verify through a separate phone number already on file—never use the phone number provided in the suspect email.
Flag and filter emails originating from external sources with 'External' email banners.
Train staff to recognize the classic 'gift card request'—CEOs do not ask junior staff to buy Apple or Google Play gift cards.
red_flags: Sudden change of remittance bank accounts to overseas or unfamiliar institutions.
Insistence on absolute secrecy ('Keep this between us until the deal closes').
Slight domain variations (e.g., acme-supplier.com instead of acmesupplier.com).
responses_en: BEC is responsible for billions in annual losses. Always establish dual-signature policies and verify changes to payment details via a confirmed verbal phone call.
intents.pro_tip_en: A 30-second phone call to verify an invoice can prevent millions of dollars in corporate wire fraud.

patterns_en: What to do if infected with ransomware
intents.summary_en: Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts your files and holds them hostage while demanding payment (usually in cryptocurrency) in exchange for a decryption key.
action_steps_en: IMMEDIATELY disconnect infected devices from Wi-Fi, Ethernet, and Bluetooth to prevent network lateral movement.
Do NOT pay the ransom—security agencies (FBI/CISA) advise against payment because it funds criminal syndicates and provides zero guarantee of file recovery.
Report the incident immediately to your IT security department, incident response team, or local cybersecurity authorities.
Maintain immutable, offline backups following the 3-2-1 backup rule (3 copies, 2 different media, 1 kept offline/offsite).
red_flags: Files suddenly changing extensions to unknown strings (e.g., .locked, .crypt, .lockbit).
Desktop background replaced with ransom instructions and countdown timers.
Antivirus or Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) software alerting on shadow copy deletion.
responses_en: Ransomware encrypts your digital assets. Disconnect the computer from all networks immediately, do not pay the ransom, notify IT security, and restore clean files from offline backups.
intents.pro_tip_en: Your strongest defense against ransomware is having an offline, air-gapped backup that cannot be reached or encrypted over the network.

patterns_en: How do I know if I have malware?
patterns_hi: मैलवेयर क्या है
intents.summary_en: Malware (malicious software) is an umbrella term covering viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware, spyware, and keyloggers designed to damage, disrupt, or gain unauthorized access to computer systems.
action_steps_en: Keep Microsoft Defender or an enterprise EDR solution active and updated.
Never download cracked software, keygens, torrents, or pirated games—they are the primary delivery vector for info-stealer malware.
Run a full anti-malware scan if your computer exhibits unexpected slowdowns, high CPU usage, or browser redirects.
Keep your operating system and browsers updated to patch known vulnerabilities (CVEs).
red_flags: Browser homepage or default search engine changing without your consent.
Frequent pop-ups, even when the web browser is closed.
Accounts being accessed from unfamiliar locations (a sign of infostealer credential theft).
responses_en: Malware encompasses all harmful software like trojans, spyware, and worms. Avoid untrusted downloads, keep automatic updates enabled, and maintain active endpoint protection.
intents.pro_tip_en: Infostealers search your browser cache for saved passwords and session cookies. Never store sensitive master passwords in your plain browser storage.

patterns_en: How to create a strong password?
Should I change my password frequently?
intents.summary_en: Strong authentication starts with high entropy: Passwords should be long, unique for every account, and unpredictable. Modern standards (NIST SP 800-63B) favor length and passphrases over complex, hard-to-remember character combinations.
action_steps_en: Use a Passphrase: Combine 4 to 5 random, unrelated words (e.g., 'correct-horse-battery-staple' or 'purple-cactus-orbit-piano!').
Aim for at least 14 to 16 characters in length—length provides exponential resistance against brute-force cracking.
NEVER reuse the same password across multiple accounts. If one service suffers a breach, attackers use automated 'credential stuffing' to breach all your accounts.
Use a dedicated Password Manager to generate and store random 20+ character passwords.
red_flags: Using personal info: birthdays, pet names, kids' names, spouse names, sports teams.
Predictable substitutions like 'P@ssw0rd2024!'. Automated cracking dictionaries guess these in milliseconds.
Writing passwords on sticky notes attached to your monitor or under your keyboard.
responses_en: Focus on length and uniqueness. Use 4-5 random words to create memorable passphrases, never reuse passwords, and let a password manager handle the rest.
intents.pro_tip_en: A 16-character passphrase made of 4 common words is vastly more secure and easier to remember than an 8-character string of random symbols.

patterns_en: What if the password manager gets hacked?
intents.summary_en: A password manager is an encrypted digital vault that generates, stores, and autofills strong, unique credentials for all your web services and applications.
action_steps_en: Adopt a reputable password manager (e.g., Bitwarden, 1Password, KeePassXC).
Create one extremely strong, memorable Master Passphrase (20+ characters) that you never write down or share.
Enable Multi-Factor Authentication (preferably with a hardware security key or authenticator app) on your password manager vault.
Leverage password managers to protect against phishing: They will not autofill your credentials if you land on a spoofed phishing URL.
red_flags: Using the browser's built-in password store without a master password lock.
Storing passwords in unencrypted Word, Excel, or Notepad files.
responses_en: Password managers are essential modern security tools. They use zero-knowledge end-to-end encryption so only you hold the decryption key. They prevent password reuse and neutralize phishing.
intents.pro_tip_en: Password managers automatically protect you against typosquatting phishing sites: if the domain is fake, the password manager simply won't offer to autofill.

intents.summary_en: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) requires two or more distinct verification factors before granting access: Something you know (password), Something you have (authenticator app, security key), and Something you are (biometrics).
action_steps_en: Enable MFA on every critical account, starting with your email, banking, and password manager.
Rank MFA methods from strongest to weakest: 1) Hardware Keys (YubiKey/FIDO2), 2) Passkeys, 3) Authenticator Apps (Google Authenticator, Aegis), 4) SMS/Email codes.
Never share your 6-digit MFA code with ANYONE over the phone, email, or chat—no legitimate technician will ask for it.
Save your one-time emergency backup recovery codes in a secure, encrypted offline location.
red_flags: Receiving unsolicited MFA prompts when you are not trying to log in (indicates your password has already been compromised).
Anyone claiming to be support asking you to 'read back the code you just received'.
responses_en: MFA adds a critical second layer of defense. Even if attackers steal your password, they cannot access your account without your physical second factor. Prefer authenticator apps or security keys over SMS.
intents.pro_tip_en: Enabling MFA blocks over 99% of automated credential-stuffing and account takeover attacks.

patterns_en: What to do if getting repeated MFA requests?
intents.summary_en: MFA Fatigue (also called MFA Bombing) is a social engineering technique where attackers who already have your password send dozens of push notifications to your phone in hopes you will accidentally tap 'Approve' to make the buzzing stop.
action_steps_en: NEVER tap 'Approve' on an unexpected MFA notification.
If you receive repeated unsolicited MFA requests, decline the prompt immediately and report it to IT security.
Change your account password immediately from a trusted device—the spammed notifications prove your password is known to attackers.
Switch to number-matching MFA (where you must type the numbers shown on the screen into your authenticator app).
red_flags: Multiple push notifications arriving late at night or during meetings.
A caller pretending to be IT claiming: 'We are sending a test prompt, please tap Approve to clear the error'.
responses_en: MFA fatigue exploits human frustration. Never approve an unprompted sign-in request. Decline the prompt and immediately change your password, because the attacker already knows it.
intents.pro_tip_en: If you tap 'Decline' on an MFA prompt, modern systems automatically trigger an alert to your company's security operations center (SOC).

intents.summary_en: Passkeys are a modern, passwordless authentication standard based on FIDO2/WebAuthn public-key cryptography. They replace passwords with cryptographic key pairs stored on your device and unlocked via biometrics (Face ID/fingerprint) or device PIN.
action_steps_en: Adopt passkeys for supported services like Google, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and GitHub.
Enjoy phishing immunity: Passkeys are cryptographically bound to the exact website domain name—they physically cannot be entered on or phished by a fake website.
Sync passkeys securely through your trusted ecosystem (Apple iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, or Bitwarden/1Password).
Keep at least two devices enrolled (e.g., your laptop and your phone) so you don't lose account access if one device is damaged.
responses_en: Passkeys replace passwords with un-phishable cryptographic keys bound to specific domains. You unlock them with your fingerprint or face scan, making credential theft practically impossible.
intents.pro_tip_en: Passkeys eliminate the possibility of phishing and credential reuse entirely. They represent the gold standard of modern identity security.

patterns_en: What is an evil twin attack?
Man in the middle attack Wi-Fi
How to stay safe on public Wi-Fi?
Should I use Wi-Fi at coffee shops?
intents.summary_en: Public Wi-Fi networks in airports, hotels, and cafes are unencrypted open networks. Attackers can snoop on unencrypted traffic, conduct Man-In-The-Middle (MITM) attacks, or set up rogue 'Evil Twin' access points with identical names.
action_steps_en: Turn off 'Auto-Connect to Open Wi-Fi' on your phone and laptop.
Use a trusted Virtual Private Network (VPN) or use your phone's cellular hotspot when performing banking or sensitive work.
Ensure every visited website displays 'HTTPS' and has no SSL certificate warnings.
Turn off File Sharing and AirDrop/Nearby Share when connected to public hotspots.
red_flags: Two identical network names (e.g., 'Starbucks_Guest' and 'Starbucks_Guest_Free').
Networks asking you to install a security certificate or download an app to gain internet access.
Browser SSL certificate warnings ('Your connection is not private').
responses_en: Public Wi-Fi can expose your device to traffic eavesdropping and rogue access points. Use a reputable VPN or cellular hotspot, ensure HTTPS connections, and disable file sharing.
intents.pro_tip_en: Your mobile phone's personal hotspot is exponentially safer than any free airport or coffee shop public Wi-Fi network.

patterns_en: Can a VPN protect against phishing?
Does a VPN make me anonymous?
intents.summary_en: A Virtual Private Network (VPN) creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and a secure server, protecting your network traffic from local eavesdroppers and disguising your IP address.
action_steps_en: Use a VPN when working on public Wi-Fi, in hotels, or connecting to company internal systems remotely.
Understand what a VPN DOES NOT DO: It does not stop phishing, it does not prevent malware downloads, and it does not make you immune to credential theft.
Choose reputable, paid, no-logs VPN providers over suspicious 'free' VPNs that sell your browsing data.
Always use your organization's official corporate VPN when accessing internal corporate applications.
responses_en: A VPN encrypts your network traffic, shielding you on untrusted public Wi-Fi networks. However, it does not stop you from falling for phishing links or downloading malware.
intents.pro_tip_en: A VPN protects your connection in transit, but if you type your password into a phishing site, a VPN will not protect you.

patterns_en: Does HTTPS mean a site is safe?
How to check if a website is legit?
intents.summary_en: Safe browsing involves inspecting domain names, understanding SSL/TLS encryption, and avoiding drive-by download traps. Crucially, HTTPS means your connection is encrypted, NOT that the website owner is honest.
action_steps_en: Inspect the domain name carefully: Check for typosquatting (e.g., paypa1.com, netfIix.com with an uppercase 'i').
Remember: Attackers use HTTPS too! Over 80% of modern phishing websites have valid SSL certificates and padlock icons.
Never bypass browser security interstitial warnings ('Deceptive site ahead').
Keep browser extensions to a minimum and audit permissions regularly.
red_flags: Websites with countdown timers demanding you claim a prize or install an update immediately.
Download prompts that initiate automatically without you clicking anything.
Unusual top-level domains (.xyz, .top, .work) used for mainstream bank or government services.
responses_en: Browsing safely means verifying domain names and not trusting a site solely because it has HTTPS. Avoid suspicious downloads, keep extensions minimal, and never ignore browser warnings.
intents.pro_tip_en: HTTPS protects data from eavesdroppers between you and the server. It does NOT guarantee that the server doesn't belong to a criminal.

intents.summary_en: Software updates and security patches fix known vulnerabilities and programming flaws (CVEs) that cybercriminals actively scan the internet to exploit.
action_steps_en: Enable automatic updates for your operating system (Windows/macOS), browsers (Chrome/Firefox/Edge), and mobile devices.
Restart your computer when updates require it—many critical patches don't take effect until the system reboot completes.
Uninstall obsolete software and old browser extensions that you no longer use.
Apply critical security patches within 24 to 48 hours of release.
red_flags: Ignoring 'Update Available' notifications for weeks at a time.
Downloading 'Flash Player' or 'Video Player' updates from pop-up banners—these are almost always malware.
responses_en: Software updates are your primary armor against known cyber exploits. Enable automatic updates, reboot promptly, and only download updates through official system settings.
intents.pro_tip_en: Over 90% of successful corporate breaches exploit software vulnerabilities for which a security patch was already available for months.

patterns_en: Encryption at rest vs in transit
intents.summary_en: Encryption scrambles plaintext data into unreadable ciphertext using mathematical algorithms and cryptographic keys, ensuring that only authorized parties holding the key can decrypt it.
action_steps_en: Enable full-disk encryption on all laptops and mobile devices (BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on macOS).
If a full-disk encrypted laptop is lost or stolen, thieves cannot read your files even if they pull out the physical hard drive.
Ensure sensitive files sent via email or cloud share are encrypted or password-protected with out-of-band key sharing.
Safeguard your BitLocker or FileVault recovery key in a secure, non-public vault.
responses_en: Encryption protects data both at rest (stored on devices) and in transit (traveling over networks). Always turn on BitLocker or FileVault so stolen hardware cannot lead to stolen data.
intents.pro_tip_en: Full disk encryption turns a stolen laptop from a devastating corporate data breach into a minor hardware replacement incident.

patterns_en: Is it safe to open zip files from email?
intents.summary_en: Email attachments and web downloads are top infection vectors for trojans, info-stealers, and ransomware. Attackers disguise executables as invoices, resumes, or shipping manifests.
action_steps_en: Examine file extensions carefully: watch out for double extensions (e.g., 'Invoice_Q3.pdf.exe' or 'Receipt.docx.vbs').
High-risk file extensions include: .exe, .scr, .iso, .vbs, .js, .bat, and .hta.
NEVER click 'Enable Content' or 'Enable Macros' on unexpected Microsoft Office documents.
If someone sends an unexpected archive (.zip or .7z) with a password in the email body, it is designed to bypass security email scanners.
red_flags: An invoice sent as an executable file (.exe or .scr) or disk image (.iso).
Documents prompting you to disable security controls to view protected content.
Unsolicited resumes or order confirmations from companies you have never contacted.
responses_en: Treat all unsolicited attachments with extreme skepticism. Watch for double extensions, never enable macros, and never open .exe or .iso files sent via email.
intents.pro_tip_en: Real invoices are almost never delivered as .zip, .iso, or .exe files. If you see those extensions, report the message immediately.

intents.summary_en: Social engineering is the psychological manipulation of people into performing actions or divulging confidential information, bypassing technical security controls.
action_steps_en: Recognize the 5 emotional triggers attackers use: 1) Urgency, 2) Fear/Intimidation, 3) Authority, 4) Curiosity/Greed, and 5) Sympathy/Helpfulness.
Slow down: Legitimate emergencies will never be jeopardized by a 2-minute independent verification.
Be willing to challenge authority politely when standard security policies are at stake.
Never plug in random USB drives found in parking lots, hallways, or lobbies (Baiting).
red_flags: Someone rushing you: 'We will lose this client if you don't send the files in 5 minutes!'.
Unfamiliar technicians asking you to disable your antivirus or read them your password.
Strangers asking you to hold open secure doors (Tailgating).
responses_en: Social engineering targets human psychology—urgency, fear, and authority. Always pause, verify unexpected requests independently, and never let emotion override security policy.
Urgency and secrecy are common manipulation tactics. Take time and verify independently.
Tailgating bypasses physical access controls. Follow your organization's visitor procedures.
One-time login codes should not be shared. Verify support requests using a known channel.
Unverified offers may be used to collect identity or workplace information.
Personal details may be publicly available and do not authenticate a caller.
Codes may authorize account access or payments. Understand the purpose and keep sensitive codes private.
Attackers impersonate authority to create urgency. Independently confirm sensitive requests before acting.
Threats and demands for immediate payment are coercive tactics. Verify independently and seek trusted help.
Unsolicited remote access can expose data and control your device. Verify support requests directly.
Procedures help prevent impersonation and unauthorized actions; don't bypass them under pressure.

अपुष्ट प्रस्तावों से पहचान या कार्यस्थल की जानकारी जुटाई जा सकती है।
व्यक्तिगत विवरण सार्वजनिक हो सकते हैं और कॉलर की पहचान प्रमाणित नहीं करते।
कोड खाते का एक्सेस या भुगतान अधिकृत कर सकते हैं। उद्देश्य समझें और संवेदनशील कोड निजी रखें।
हमलावर जल्दबाजी के लिए अधिकारी होने का रूप लेते हैं। संवेदनशील अनुरोध पर कार्रवाई से पहले अलग से पुष्टि करें।
धमकी और तुरंत भुगतान की मांग दबाव के तरीके हैं। स्वयं पुष्टि करें और विश्वसनीय सहायता लें।
अनचाहा रिमोट एक्सेस डेटा उजागर कर सकता है और डिवाइस नियंत्रित कर सकता है। सहायता अनुरोध की सीधे पुष्टि करें।
प्रक्रियाएं पहचान की नकल और अनधिकृत कार्रवाई रोकती हैं; दबाव में इन्हें न छोड़ें।
intents.pro_tip_en: Attackers hack humans because humans are easier to exploit than 256-bit AES encryption. When an email or call induces sudden anxiety, that emotion is your warning alarm.

intents.summary_en: Physical security protects hardware, paper records, and workspaces from unauthorized access. A clean desk policy ensures sensitive information is not exposed to passersby, visitors, or cleaners.
action_steps_en: Always lock your screen (Windows Key + L or Mac Ctrl + Cmd + Q) every single time you step away from your desk.
Never leave company laptops, access badges, or sensitive client files visible in parked cars or unattended conference rooms.
Do not allow 'Tailgating': ensure every person swipes their own security badge at building access doors.
Shred sensitive physical documents using cross-cut shredders rather than throwing them into standard recycling bins.
red_flags: Sticky notes containing passwords stuck to monitors or under keyboards.
Unknown individuals wandering corporate corridors without visitor badges.
Printed confidential payroll or HR documents left unattended on shared printers.
responses_en: Digital safety requires physical vigilance. Lock your workstation every time you step away (Win+L), safeguard access badges, shred sensitive paperwork, and prevent unauthorized tailgating.
intents.pro_tip_en: Make locking your workstation a physical reflex: fingers on 'Win+L' whenever your feet leave your chair.

intents.summary_en: USB flash drives can carry malware or hardware exploits (BadUSB) that disguise themselves as keyboards and execute malicious command-line payloads within seconds. Public USB charging ports can also be modified to steal data ('Juice Jacking').
action_steps_en: NEVER plug an unknown or unverified USB drive into your computer—give it directly to IT security.
Use your own AC wall charger or an external power bank rather than public USB charging kiosks in airports.
If you must charge from public USB ports, use a 'USB Data Blocker' (a hardware adapter that physically disconnects data pins).
Organizations should enforce USB device control policies to restrict unauthorized removable media.
red_flags: Promotional USB drives handed out by unknown vendors or left in public lobbies.
Phones prompting 'Trust this computer?' when plugged into a public charging station.
responses_en: Never plug in unknown USB flash drives—they can execute malicious code in seconds. For public charging, use standard AC wall outlets or a hardware USB data blocker.
intents.pro_tip_en: A BadUSB does not look like a virus to your computer; it registers as an ultra-fast keyboard typing malicious PowerShell commands at 1,000 words per minute.

intents.summary_en: Working from home expands the corporate security perimeter to your home network. Vulnerable routers, default credentials, and smart IoT devices can become attack footholds.
action_steps_en: Change default router credentials (both the admin password and the Wi-Fi WPA3/WPA2 passphrase).
Create a separate Guest Wi-Fi network for smart home gadgets (IoT cameras, smart bulbs, smart TVs) to isolate them from work devices.
Keep work data strictly on company-issued devices; avoid forwarding work emails to personal email accounts.
Ensure your home router's firmware is updated and remote management features are turned off.
responses_en: Secure your remote workplace: Change default router passwords, isolate smart IoT gadgets on a guest Wi-Fi network, and conduct all business solely on managed corporate devices.
intents.pro_tip_en: Putting your smart home appliances and IoT devices on a dedicated Guest Wi-Fi network prevents a hacked smart lightbulb from compromising your work laptop.

intents.summary_en: Smartphones hold immense amounts of personal, biometric, and corporate data. Protecting them requires minimal app permissions, verified app stores, and remote wipe capabilities.
action_steps_en: Install apps only from official stores (Apple App Store, Google Play); avoid sideloading APK files from third-party websites.
Review app permissions regularly: Revoke access to microphone, camera, contacts, and precise location for apps that do not need them.
Enable 'Find My Device' / 'Find My iPhone' with remote wipe enabled in case of theft.
Set a strong 6-digit PIN or passphrase (avoid 1234 or 0000) combined with biometric face or fingerprint lock.
red_flags: Battery draining rapidly or phone overheating when idle (a symptom of background spyware).
Unexplained spikes in mobile data consumption.
Strange pop-up windows appearing across your home screen.
responses_en: Keep mobile devices protected: Use strong PINs, review app permissions, only install from official app stores, and enable remote locate/wipe capabilities.
intents.pro_tip_en: Rebooting your smartphone once a day flushes many zero-click, in-memory spyware implants that do not possess persistent boot storage.

intents.summary_en: Immediate action can prevent a minor error from escalating into a full organizational breach. Don't panic, don't hide the mistake, and act quickly.
action_steps_en: DISCONNECT IMMEDIATELY: Unplug the network cable (Ethernet) or turn off Wi-Fi on the affected device to halt malware transmission.
CHANGE PASSWORDS (from a DIFFERENT, uncompromised device): Change the password for the affected account and terminate all other active sessions.
REPORT TO IT / SECURITY: Contact your organization's IT Helpdesk or Security Operations Center (SOC) immediately. Quick reporting is valued, not punished.
DO NOT DELETE EVIDENCE: Keep the phishing email, headers, and transaction timestamps so analysts can block the threat across the company.
CONTACT YOUR BANK: If financial data or debit/credit cards were entered, notify the bank immediately to freeze the card.
red_flags: Attempting to cover up the mistake or delay reporting—delays allow attackers time to establish persistence and steal data.
responses_en: Immediate steps: Disconnect the device from Wi-Fi/Ethernet, change your passwords from a clean device, report the incident to IT security right away, and preserve the suspicious message for evidence.
intents.pro_tip_en: Security teams deal with clicked links every single day. The faster you report it, the faster they can contain the impact and protect your colleagues.

intents.summary_en: Account takeover occurs when an unauthorized user gains access to your cloud account. Prompt session revocation and recovery audits are vital.
action_steps_en: Go to your account's Security settings and click 'Log out of all other sessions' / 'Revoke active devices'.
Change your account password to a new, unique 16+ character passphrase.
Audit your account's Recovery email address and Recovery phone number to verify the attacker did not change them to their own.
Check for malicious email forwarding rules (attackers frequently configure silent inbox rules to forward your sensitive emails to themselves).
Enable an Authenticator App or Passkey for MFA.
red_flags: Sent emails or direct messages that you never wrote.
Notifications of password resets or sign-ins originating from foreign countries or unfamiliar devices.
New mailbox rules that automatically redirect incoming emails to the Trash or RSS folder.
responses_en: To reclaim a compromised account: Revoke all active sessions, change your password immediately, verify recovery details, check for hidden email forwarding rules, and enable MFA.
intents.pro_tip_en: Always check your email forwarding rules after an account scare; sneaky forwarding rules are how attackers maintain quiet access even after password changes.

intents.summary_en: Data breaches occur when corporate databases containing customer credentials or personal identifiable information (PII) are stolen or leaked online.
action_steps_en: Check HaveIBeenPwned.com to see if your email address or passwords have appeared in public data breaches.
Place a FREE Credit Freeze with the three major credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) to prevent criminals from opening unauthorized loans in your name.
Change any passwords that match the leaked credentials immediately across all accounts.
Set up transaction alerts on bank accounts and credit cards to detect fraudulent charges instantly.
responses_en: After a breach: Check your exposure on HaveIBeenPwned, change exposed passwords, turn on MFA, and place a free credit freeze across major credit reporting bureaus.
intents.pro_tip_en: A credit freeze is free by law, takes 10 minutes to set up, and is the single most effective barrier against identity theft.

intents.summary_en: Shadow IT is the use of unapproved hardware, cloud services, or software without the knowledge or approval of corporate IT. Insider threats stem from employees or contractors who misuse or accidentally leak internal data.
action_steps_en: Never forward confidential company spreadsheets, code, or client lists to personal email or personal cloud storage.
Request approval from IT before using new AI tools, software apps, or collaboration platforms.
Understand that personal services lack enterprise security controls, DLP monitoring, and data retention compliance.
Report inadvertent data leaks to IT security immediately so they can be contained.
red_flags: Pasting proprietary company source code, financial roadmaps, or customer PII into public AI tools.
Sharing company Google Drive or OneDrive links configured with 'Anyone with the link can edit'.
responses_en: Avoid Shadow IT by using only authorized company tools for business data. Never forward company assets to personal accounts or unvetted cloud storage.
intents.pro_tip_en: Most insider data breaches are not malicious sabotage—they are well-meaning employees trying to work faster using unvetted personal tools.

responses_en: A UPI PIN authorizes money leaving your account; it is not needed to receive money.
A collect request asks you to pay. Approve only if you recognize and intend the payment.
Screenshots can be altered. Confirm payments in your own bank or UPI transaction history.

Contact your bank or app provider quickly; never pay a third party promising guaranteed recovery.
Review the transaction wording and recipient. A payment request is not a refund credit.
Always check the recipient and amount on the confirmation screen before entering your PIN.
Fraudsters use fake safe-account stories to steal money. Banks do not ask customers to move funds this way.
Promptly report unauthorized debits to your bank and use official reporting channels.
Keep your UPI PIN secret. It authorizes payments from your account.

PIN डालने से पहले पुष्टि स्क्रीन पर प्राप्तकर्ता और राशि हमेशा जांचें।

responses_en: Unique passwords prevent one exposed account from unlocking others.
A reputable password manager can create and store unique passwords; protect it with a strong master password and MFA.
Replace exposed passwords with unique ones and enable multi-factor authentication.
Long, unique passphrases are harder to guess, especially when not reused.
Security answers can be guessed from public details; treat them as secret credentials.
Recovery codes can bypass account protections, so keep them private and securely stored.
Legitimate support should not need your password. Never disclose it to another person.
MFA requires another proof of identity, making a stolen password less useful to an attacker.
Reusing a password lets an attacker try leaked credentials on other services.
Secure the account promptly, end unknown sessions, and use MFA to reduce further access.

दिखाया गया प्राप्तकर्ता अनपेक्षित हो तो भुगतान अधिकृत न करें। आगे बढ़ने से पहले पुष्टि करें।
intents.pro_tip_en: Always verify transactions and unexpected communications regarding QR Code Scams.
intents.pro_tip_hi: QR कोड धोखाधड़ी से जुड़े किसी भी अनपेक्षित संदेश या कॉल की पहले आधिकारिक स्रोत से पुष्टि करें।

patterns_hi: सोशल मीडिया क्या है?
सोशल मीडिया से कैसे बचें?
सोशल मीडिया धोखाधड़ी के बारे में बताएं
सोशल मीडिया सुरक्षा नियम
मित्र की फोटो वाला नया खाता आपातकालीन पैसे मांगता है। क्या करें?
सोशल मीडिया क्विज़ जन्मदिन, पहले स्कूल और पालतू का नाम मांगता है। क्या ध्यान रखें?
सीधा संदेश कहता है कि लिंक से लॉगिन न करने पर खाता बंद होगा। क्या करें?
साधारण वॉलपेपर सुविधा वाला सोशल ऐप संपर्क, माइक्रोफोन और स्थान एक्सेस मांगता है। क्या करें?
सोशल मीडिया खाते को सुरक्षित करने का अच्छा तरीका क्या है?
पोस्ट मुफ्त डेटा पाने के लिए लिंक शेयर करके दूसरी सेवा से लॉगिन करने को कहती है। क्या करें?
आपको ऐसा MFA स्वीकृति अनुरोध आता है जिसे आपने शुरू नहीं किया। क्या करें?
अजनबी आपकी फोटो होने का दावा करके फाइल भेजता है। क्या करें?

सोशल मीडिया पर अनजान व्यक्ति लाइव लोकेशन मांगता है। क्या करें?
सोशल मीडिया फ्रॉड क्या है
